Content: The teacher drew this model of the sugar and water particles after the sugar was added to the water. The teacher used black circles to represent sugar particles and white circles to represent water particles.
problems/OKG5S/media/1a.jpg
Which model shows the mixture in the jar when the sugar was no longer visible?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/1b.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that sugar particles and water particles should be represented differently.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/1c.jpg

Key.Rationale: There are different representations for sugar particles and water particles and the `text(two)` types of particles are mixed together.

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/1d.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that sugar particles and water particles should be represented differently.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/1e.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that the sugar and water particles would not be divided into `text(two)` separate groups; they should be mixed together.

Content: Which statement `bbtext(best)` describes how sugar crystals formed during the investigation?

A.Choice: It took a long time for sugar to form in water.

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that the amount of time does not describe how the sugar crystals formed.

B.Choice: Sugar particles were destroyed when the water was stirred.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that dissolving destroys matter.

C.Choice: Sugar particles collected together until they were big enough to see.

Key.Rationale: While dissolved in water, sugar particles are too small to be seen; as sugar particles come out of solution, the particles grow in size until they are visible.

D.Choice: The amount of sugar inside the jar increased when the stick was added.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that so much sugar was added that sugar particles were visible.

Content: What should a model show to `bbtext(best)` explain how the sugar became no longer visible?

A.Choice: sugar collecting

Key.Rationale: The sugar collecting together would be larger and easier to see.

B.Choice: sugar evaporating

Key.Rationale: The sugar doesn't evaporate.

C.Choice: sugar changing into water

Key.Rationale: The sugar doesn't become water.

D.Choice: sugar breaking into pieces

Key.Rationale: The sugar breaks into particles too small to be seen.

Content: The students measured `text(each material)` before stirring them together. The students slowly stirred the lemonade mix and sugar into the glass of water. The lemonade mix and sugar both seemed to disappear. Several students thought the amount of matter changed when the lemonade mix and sugar disappeared. The students decide to measure the mixture to find out if the amount of matter changed.
Which statement best explains which tool should be used to show what happens to the amount of matter after the mixture is stirred?

A.Choice: The students should use a scale which will show that the total weight stayed the same.

Key.Rationale: The amount of matter is measured using mass/weight. Matter is conserved so the weight will remain the same.

B.Choice: The students should use a measuring cup which will show that the total volume stayed the same.

Key.Rationale: The student may have thought that matter was measured using volume.

C.Choice: The students should use a scale which will show that the total weight decreased.

Key.Rationale: The student may have thought that the amount of matter decreased when the substances dissolved.

D.Choice: The students should use a measuring cup which will show that the total volume decreased.

Key.Rationale: The student may have thought that matter was measured using volume.

Content: The students removed the lemon ice from the ice cube tray at the end of the investigation. Then they measured the total weight of all the lemon ice cubes.
Which graph shows the total weight of the liquid lemonade before it was poured into the tray and the total weight of the lemon ice removed from the tray?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/5a.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the mass of the water and the lemonade mix is not included in the liquid lemonade or that the mass of lemon ice is greater because its size is greater.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/5b.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the mass of the lemonade mix is not included in the liquid lemonade or that the mass of lemon ice is greater because its size is greater.

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/5c.jpg

Key.Rationale: Freezing lemonade does not change the mass.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/5d.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the mass of the lemonade mix and the sugar is not included in the lemon ice.

Content: The students decided to let the lemon ice melt after the investigation. Once the lemon ice melted, the students poured all the liquid into a different ice cube tray. The drawing below shows this new tray.
problems/OKG5S/media/6a.jpg

The students poured the same amount of lemonade into `text(each spot)` in the tray. There was no lemonade left over. The students covered the tray and placed it in the freezer overnight. The students removed the tray from the freezer the next day.
Which statement is correct about the new lemon ice cubes?

A.Choice: The new lemon ice weighed less than the lemon ice made the `text(first)` time.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that smaller ice cubes result in less total mass.

B.Choice: `text(Each new lemon ice cube)` had the same weight as `text(each lemon ice cube)` made the `text(first)` time.

Key.Rationale: The student may confuse the conservation of mass with the mass of the different sized ice cubes.

C.Choice: `text(Each new lemon ice cube)` contained more matter than `text(each lemon ice cube)` made the `text(first)` time.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that more ice cubes results in each having more mass.

D.Choice: The new lemon ice contained the same amount of matter as the lemon ice made the `text(first)` time.

Key.Rationale: The total amount of matter stays the same throughout these steps.

Content: The student carried out `text(three)` tests with a white baking substance. They mixed the substance with water. Then they mixed the substance with vinegar. Finally, they heated the substance. The student recorded the observations shown.

:ibox:• Small crystals
• Dissolved in water
• No bubbles in vinegar
• No change when heated
Which substance did the student have?

A.Choice: Baking soda

Key.Rationale: Baking soda does not change when heated and it does bubble in vinegar.

B.Choice: Flour

Key.Rationale: Flour does not dissolve in water and does not look like small crystals.

C.Choice: Sugar

Key.Rationale: Granulated sugar does melt.

D.Choice: Salt

Key.Rationale: Salt is the only substance that exhibits all `text(four)` properties the student observed for the white powder.

Content: The student compared the `text(two)` sugars.
Which statement explains how the student could tell the difference between the `text(two)` types of sugars?

A.Choice: by stirring both sugars into a cup of water

Key.Rationale: This will not allow the student to differentiate between the `text(two)` sugars because both sugars dissolve in water.

B.Choice: by heating both sugars

Key.Rationale: The properties the student will examine will differentiate the sugars from the other powders but not from each other as they both turn brown when heated.

C.Choice: by viewing both sugars under a hand lens

Key.Rationale: The hand lens will allow the student to see that `text(one)` sugar is made up of crystals and the other of powder.

D.Choice: by adding both sugars to vinegar

Key.Rationale: Neither sugar bubbles in vinegar and therefore the student will not be able to differentiate between the `text(two)` types of sugar.

Content: The student had a substance that did not bubble in vinegar and wanted to see if they could figure out what the substance was by only using heat. The student noticed that some of the substances have multiple reactions when heated.
Which statement explains if the student was able to tell what substance they had from using only the `text(two)` properties?

A.Choice: The student will be able to tell the difference because powder sugar turns brown when heated.

Key.Rationale: Both sugars turn brown when heated, therefore if the substance the student is testing is sugar, they will not be able to tell the difference.

B.Choice: The student will be able to tell the difference because salt and sugar are both crystal in appearance.

Key.Rationale: The student is using the wrong property to determine what the substance is.

C.Choice: The student will not be able to tell the difference because flour is powder in appearance and sugar is crystal in appearance.

Key.Rationale: The student is using the wrong property to determine what the substance is.

D.Choice: The student will not be able to tell the difference because both sugars turn brown when heated.

Key.Rationale: The student will not be able to tell what the substance is by only using the `text(two)` properties because both sugars turn brown when heated and do not bubble in vinegar.

Content: The students claim that a new substance formed in Mixture `2`.
Which observation from the students' investigation supports this claim?

A.Choice: The mixture is a liquid.

Key.Rationale: The state of the mixture is irrelevant to whether a new substance formed.

B.Choice: The mixture has lemon juice.

Key.Rationale: This information about what substances were combined to form the mixture does not indicate whether a new substance formed.

C.Choice: Bubbles are present in the mixture.

Key.Rationale: Bubbles indicate that gas formed, which would support the students' claim that a new substance formed.

D.Choice: Solids are not present in the mixture.

Key.Rationale: This observation would not support the students' claim because it would indicate that a new solid substance did not form.

Content: The students make a `text(fourth)` mixture by mixing water and an unknown solid in a bottle and placing a balloon on the opening of the bottle.
Which observation would `bbtext(best)` help the students determine that a new substance may have been formed in Mixture `4`?

A.Choice: After mixing, the solid dissolved in water.

Key.Rationale: A solid can dissolve in a liquid without forming a new substance.

B.Choice: After mixing, the balloon remained unfilled.

Key.Rationale: This evidence would suggest that a gas did not form to fill the balloon, which would indicate that a new substance did not form.

C.Choice: After mixing, the resulting liquid looked clear.

Key.Rationale: Substances can change appearance in mixtures without a new substance forming.

D.Choice: After mixing, there was a temperature change.

Key.Rationale: A change in temperature can provide evidence that a chemical reaction occurred and therefore a new substance formed.

Content: The students want to change their investigation to gather evidence that a new substance formed.
Which change to their investigation procedure would `bbtext(best)` help the students gather evidence of a new substance forming?

A.Choice: Mix different amounts of `text(each substance)` in `text(each mixture)`.

Key.Rationale: The amount of `text(each substance)` mixed is irrelevant to whether new substances form afterward and the variable of how much `text(each substance)` is mixed would not be controlled to gather reliable evidence.

B.Choice: Increase the amount of `text(each substance)` in `text(each mixture)`.

Key.Rationale: Changing the amount of substance mixed would not affect the outcome of the same substances being combined together and may not result in a new substance forming.

C.Choice: Determine whether some of the substances remain solid after becoming part of `text(each mixture)`.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that after a chemical reaction, the product is a mixture in which some of the substances remain unchanged.

D.Choice: Record whether there is a difference between the properties of `text(each substance)` and the mixture.

Key.Rationale: Measuring whether there was a change in properties could indicate whether a new substance formed as a result of substances being mixed.

Content: Which observation during the experiment `bbtext(best)` supports the claim that gravity pulls objects toward the center of `text(Earth)`?

A.Choice: The paper clips swing freely when the ruler is tilted.

Key.Rationale: The swinging doesn't indicate that the gravitational force pulls objects toward the center of `text(Earth)`.

B.Choice: The paper clips are all the same distance from the tilted ruler.

Key.Rationale: The distance, which is directed by the string, doesn't indicate that the gravitational force pulls objects toward the center of Earth.

C.Choice: The paper clips hang straight down no matter how the ruler is tilted.

Key.Rationale: This shows that gravity pulls the object straight down toward `text(Earth's)` center.

D.Choice: The paper clips remain attached to the ruler no matter how the ruler is tilted.

Key.Rationale: The attachment doesn't indicate that the gravitational force pulls objects toward the center of `text(Earth)`.

Content: How could the experiment be revised to best provide additional evidence to support the claim that `text(Earth's)` gravity pulls objects toward the center of `text(Earth)`?

A.Choice: Repeat the experiment with a wooden ruler.

Key.Rationale: The material the ruler is made out of doesn't affect gravity.

B.Choice: Repeat the experiment outside on a windy day.

Key.Rationale: This could affect the strings hanging straight down if the wind blows them.

C.Choice: Repeat the experiment in different places on `text(Earth)`.

Key.Rationale: If the experiment shows that everywhere on `text(Earth)` objects fall toward the ground, then that lends support to the claim that gravity pulls objects toward the center of the `text(Earth)`.

D.Choice: Repeat the experiment on different planets in our solar system.

Key.Rationale: Repeating the experiment on other planets will show the effect of those planets' gravity on the paper clips.

Content: The students cut the string on the `text(first)` paperclip from the tilted ruler.
Select the location where the paper clip will fall when the string is cut and provide the `bbtext(best)` explanation for your selection.
problems/OKG5S/media/15a.jpg

A.Choice: Position `Z` because the ruler is tilted

Key.Rationale: The ruler being tilted will not affect where the paper clip falls on the ground.

B.Choice: Position `X` because the `text(Earth's)` gravity pulls objects downward towards the center of the `text(Earth)`

Key.Rationale: The paper clip will fall straight down to Position `X` because `text(Earth's)` gravity pulls objects downward to the center of the `text(Earth)`.

C.Choice: Position `Y` because the ruler is tilted

Key.Rationale: The ruler being tilted will not affect where the paper clip falls on the ground.

D.Choice: Position `W` because the `text(Earth's)` gravity pulls objects downward towards the center of the `text(Earth)`

Key.Rationale: The paper clips will not fall to Position `W` because it is not straight below the paper clip that has the string being cut.

Content: Based on the Desert Ecosystem Food Web, which statement describes the movement of energy in this ecosystem?

A.Choice: Snakes get energy from squirrels and provide it to hawks.

Key.Rationale: The food web indicates that snakes eat squirrels and hawks eat snakes, so energy is transferred from squirrels to snakes to hawks.

B.Choice: Hawks get energy from snakes and provide it to squirrels.

Key.Rationale: The food web indicates that hawks eat squirrels, so energy is transferred from squirrels to hawks.

C.Choice: Brittlebrush gets energy from mice and squirrels and provides it to hawks.

Key.Rationale: The food web indicates that mice and squirrels eat brittlebrush, and hawks eat mice and squirrels, so energy is transferred from brittlebrush to mice and squirrels to hawks.

D.Choice: Squirrels get energy from snakes and hawks and provide it to brittlebrush.

Key.Rationale: The food web indicates that snakes eat mice and mice eat brittlebrush, so energy is transferred from brittlebrush to mice to snakes to hawks.

Content: Which statement about the Desert Ecosystem Food Web `bbtext(best)` describes the original source of energy for hawks in this ecosystem?

A.Choice: brittlebrush, because hawks get energy directly from brittlebrush

Key.Rationale: Plants like brittlebrush derive their energy from the `text(Sun)` and hawks do not eat brittlebrush, but instead eat the mice and squirrels that eat brittlebrush.

B.Choice: mice, because hawks eat mice and this food helps hawks grow

Key.Rationale: Mice are not the original source of energy in this ecosystem since energy is transferred from the `text(Sun)` to brittlebrush plants and then to mice.

C.Choice: the soil, because brittlebrush gets energy from the soil and hawks gain that energy when they eat brittlebrush

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that brittlebrush plants get their energy from the soil rather than the `text(Sun)` and that hawks directly eat brittlebrush instead of eating the mice and squirrels that eat brittlebrush plants.

D.Choice: the `text(Sun)`, because brittlebrush uses energy from the `text(Sun)` to grow and hawks gain that energy when they eat mice

Key.Rationale: All organisms in the food web either directly or indirectly eat plants, like brittlebrush, and plants obtain their energy from the `text(Sun)`.

Content: The student learns that while deserts can be very hot during the day, they can be very cold at night. While thinking about this information, the student wonders how squirrels would be affected at night if there were no brittlebrush plants in the desert.
Based on the Desert Ecosystem Food Web, which statement `bbtext(best)` describes how squirrels would be affected in a desert ecosystem without brittlebrush plants?

A.Choice: Squirrels would get energy they need from the air to stay warm on cold nights.

Key.Rationale: Squirrels do not obtain energy from the air but instead from eating brittlebrush plants, and that food provides squirrels with the energy they need to maintain body warmth.

B.Choice: Squirrels would not need the energy they get from hawks to stay warm on cold nights.

Key.Rationale: Squirrels eat brittlebrush plants, not hawks.

C.Choice: Squirrels would not get the energy from food that is needed to stay warm on cold nights.

Key.Rationale: The food web indicates that energy is transferred from brittlebrush plants to squirrels and the food that squirrels eat provides them with the energy needed to maintain body warmth.

D.Choice: Squirrels would need to make their own energy from sunlight to stay warm on cold nights.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that squirrels can make their own food like plants.

Content: The students also learned what some of the organisms eat.

:ibox:• Prairie chickens eat native grasses and coyotes eat prairie chickens.
• Native grasses are eaten by antelope and antelope are eaten by coyotes.
Match `text(each organism)` to a box in the food web to show how matter moves among the organism.
problems/OKG5S/media/19a.jpg
What can the students add to their model to show that matter also moves between organisms and the environment?

A.Choice: rocks, because they are a common part of soil

Key.Rationale: The student may think that rocks in the soil will show movement of matter.

B.Choice: `text(Sun)`, because it allows plants to make their own food

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the `text(Sun)` provides matter for organisms.

C.Choice: wind, because it moves air and dust around the grassland

Key.Rationale: The student may think that wind will show movement of matter into organisms.

D.Choice: decomposers, because they break down dead plants and animals

Key.Rationale: Decomposers (an organism) move matter from organisms into the environment.

Content: Which set of events should the students' model also include to show how matter moves in the ecosystem?

A.Choice: Plants take up air and water to make food. `->` Animals eat plants. `->` Animals breathe out air.

Key.Rationale: This traces part of the path carbon takes in an ecosystem.

B.Choice: Plants release food as waste. `->` Animals break down waste from plants. `->` Animals breathe out air.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that plants make food as waste and that animals break down waste from plants.

C.Choice: Animals take in air and water to make food. `->` Other animals eat these animals. `->` Animals release waste.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that animals make food.

D.Choice: Animals release waste into air. `->` Water is taken up by animals to make food. `->` Other animals eat these animals.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that animals make food and that animals exhale water.

Content: During the year, the number of `text(hours)` Orion can be seen in Oklahoma changes.
Which graph correctly shows the changes?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/22a.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think the values should increase from left to right and incorrectly interprets some of the numbers in the data table.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/22b.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think the values should increase from left to right and that the values in the graph should not match what is in the data table.

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/22c.jpg

Key.Rationale: This graph has a proper `ytext(-axis)` and correctly matches the data from the table to the data shown in the graph.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/22d.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that they should round the values in the graph to the nearest integer.

Content: Some `text(months)` are missing from the student's data table.
Which table shows the number of `text(hours)` Orion will likely be seen in `text(September)` and `text(November)` in Oklahoma?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/23a.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the time Orion is visible `text(each month)` after the months shown in the table should be less than the previous month.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/23b.jpg

Key.Rationale: The `text(September)` value is between the `text(August)` and `text(October)` values while the `text(November)` value is between the `text(October)` and `text(December)` values.

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/23c.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that the time Orion is visible `text(each month)` after the months shown in the table should be significantly less than the previous month.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/23d.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that `text(September)` is a month that Orion is visible for a peak amount of time before decreasing into `text(October)` and `text(November)`.

Content: Which graph shows the number of hours Bootes will `bbtext(most likely)` be seen in the Oklahoma night sky during the `text(year)`?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/24a.jpg

Key.Rationale: Given the location of Bootes relative to Orion and the Orion data, this graph shows the amount of time Bootes will be visible `text(each month)`.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/24b.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that Bootes will have the same amount of visible time as Orion.

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/24c.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that Bootes has an increasing visibility time throughout a calendar year.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/24d.jpg

Key.Rationale: The student may think that Bootes will be offset `6` `text(months)` relative to Orion, rather than `3` `text(months)`.

Content: Step `A` shows one way water can move into the air before it falls as rain.
Which statement `bbtext(best)` explains this process?

A.Choice: Gravity changes water from liquid to gas.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that gravity is responsible for evaporation.

B.Choice: Gravity changes water from gas to liquid.

Key.Rationale: The student may think that gravity is responsible for evaporation and may not understand that evaporation changes water from a liquid to a gas.

C.Choice: The `text(Sun)`'s energy changes water from liquid to gas.

Key.Rationale: Heat from the `text(Sun)` evaporates water from liquid into gas.

D.Choice: The `text(Sun)`'s energy changes water from gas to liquid.

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that evaporation changes water from a liquid to a gas.

Content: Which model `bbtext(best)` shows how water moves between `text(Earth)` systems to create rainfall on an island?

A.Choice: `text(atmosphere)->text(hydrosphere)->text(geosphere)`

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that rain falls from the atmosphere to the geosphere.

B.Choice: `text(hydrosphere)->text(atmosphere)->text(geosphere)`

Key.Rationale: Water from ocean evaporation (hydrosphere to atmosphere) condenses and falls as rain on the island (atmosphere to geosphere).

C.Choice: `text(biosphere)->text(geosphere)->text(hydrosphere)`

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that water will need to move through the atmosphere for it to rain.

D.Choice: `text(geosphere)->text(biosphere)->text(hydrosphere)`

Key.Rationale: The student may be confused with how many plants get their water from the geosphere.

Content: Step `text(F)` of the water cycle model represents which movement between `text(Earth)` systems?

A.Choice: Water moves as a gas from the biosphere to the atmosphere.

Key.Rationale: Water transpires as a gas from plants (biosphere) into the atmosphere.

B.Choice: Water moves as a gas from the hydrosphere to the biosphere.

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand the direction that water is moving in Step `text(F)`.

C.Choice: Water moves as a liquid from the biosphere to the geosphere.

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that water moves as a gas in Step `text(F)`, and that it is moving into the atmosphere.

D.Choice: Water moves as a liquid from the geosphere to the hydrosphere.

Key.Rationale: The student may not understand that water moves as a gas in Step `text(F)`, and may be confused with the process by which many trees get their water from the ground.

Content: Which statement could the student make to `text(best)` describe freshwater sources on `text(Earth)`?

A.Choice: Most of `text(Earth's)` fresh water is in lakes, rivers, streams, and wetlands.

Key.Rationale: Most of `text(Earth's)` fresh water is in glaciers or groundwater.

B.Choice: There is a smaller fraction of `text(Earth's)` fresh water in the ocean than in groundwater.

Key.Rationale: Students may have the misconception that the ocean is fresh water rather than salt water and that most fresh water is in lakes, rivers, streams, wetlands, glaciers, ice caps, and permanent snow instead of groundwater.

C.Choice: Most of `text(Earth's)` fresh water is in ice caps, glaciers, permanent snow, and groundwater.

Key.Rationale: This represents the correct distribution of `text(Earth's)` fresh water, with most of it in glaciers and groundwater and the rest, a small fraction, in lakes, rivers, streams, and wetlands.

D.Choice: There is a smaller fraction of `text(Earth's)` fresh water in ice caps, glaciers, and permanent snow than in other freshwater sources.

Key.Rationale: Students may not recognize that most fresh water is in ice caps, glaciers, and permanent snow rather than in other freshwater sources.

Content: Based on the `text(Earth's)` Water Volume table, the student wonders how the amount of groundwater on `text(Earth)` compares to the amount of water in the ocean.
Which bar graph represents `text(Earth's)` water sources by comparing the total volume of groundwater to the total volume of `text(Earth's)` ocean?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/29a.jpg

Key.Rationale: Groundwater is a large freshwater source but is not so large that it would be half as much as the volume of ocean water since fresh water is still a much smaller fraction of `text(Earth's)` total water volume.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/29b.jpg

Key.Rationale: Groundwater is a much smaller fraction of `text(Earth's)` total water volume compared to the ocean, since most of the water on `text(Earth)` is salt water (the ocean).

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/29c.jpg

Key.Rationale: Groundwater is a freshwater source and is therefore a much smaller fraction of `text(Earth's)` total water volume than the ocean, so those water volumes are not equal.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/29d.jpg

Key.Rationale: The ocean makes up the vast majority of `text(Earth's)` total water volume, so groundwater cannot have a larger water volume than ocean water.

Content: Based on the `text(Earth's)` Water Volume table, the student wonders how the amount of salt water on `text(Earth)` compares with the amount of fresh water.
Which bar graph represents the comparison of saltwater and freshwater sources on `text(Earth)`?

A.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/30a.jpg

Key.Rationale: The ocean makes up the vast majority of `text(Earth's)` water and consists of salt water, so there is much more salt water than fresh water on `text(Earth)`.

B.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/30b.jpg

Key.Rationale: Students may think that the ocean is fresh water rather than salt water.

C.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/30c.jpg

Key.Rationale: Students do not recognize that there is much more salt water on `text(Earth)` (the ocean) rather than fresh water.

D.Choice: problems/OKG5S/media/30d.jpg

Key.Rationale: There is more salt water than fresh water on `text(Earth)` but fresh water is a very small fraction, much smaller than half the amount of `text(Earth's)` total saltwater volume.
